design_detail: Narrative review by nine vascular-biology and clinical authors at LSU Health Sciences Center, Shreveport, in Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology (2019;39(9):1739–1746). Sections: pharmacology and binding sites; vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension; atherosclerotic disease; arrhythmias; cardiomyopathy; summary and future directions; highlights. There is no methods section: no search strategy, eligibility criteria or appraisal of the cited studies. 64 references. Most mechanistic statements rest on rodent, ex vivo and cell-culture work; only five passages give numbers from human studies. Two schematic figures and a graphical abstract (images; legends read). Read as the NIH author manuscript deposited in PMC.
can_establish: Which mechanisms and which human, animal and cell studies these authors considered relevant to methamphetamine and cardiovascular disease in 2019, and where they themselves judged the evidence to be thin.
cannot_establish: How common any cardiovascular outcome is in people who use methamphetamine, or by how much methamphetamine raises its risk, because no search, selection criteria or appraisal is reported, the few human figures are second-hand, unadjusted and without intervals, and much of the causal account comes from rodent and cell experiments.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited human evidence: autopsy and coronial series from the USA and Australia (refs 14, 40, 41, 50), a US National Inpatient Sample analysis published as a meeting abstract (ref 49), a 20-versus-21 comparison of vasodilator function (ref 31), a human laboratory study of cardiovascular response (ref 24), a single ECG study (ref 52), case reports and clinical series of cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension (refs 32, 33, 51, 54, 55, 59–61). Animal evidence: mouse, rat and one other animal model (refs 25–27, 42, 43, 53, 56, 62). Cell and tissue evidence: endothelial cells, macrophages, T lymphocytes, cardiomyocytes, rat aorta (refs 29, 30, 34, 36, 39, 45, 46, 48, 57, 58, 63, 64).
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated and cannot be audited. All the human figures come from people who died or reached hospital (autopsy, coronial and inpatient records, case series), so they describe severe end-points in selected groups, not risk in people who use methamphetamine. Several statements carry no citation at all (see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The review does not say how methamphetamine use was established in any cited human study (self-report, toxicology or records).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The review cites plasma concentrations averaging 2–3 μM in people who use methamphetamine, up to 17 μM in people arrested for erratic behaviour and 87 μM in post-mortem samples from deaths not due to overdose (refs 21–23), and compares them with binding values at the dopamine transporter (Ki 0.46 μM), noradrenaline transporter (Ki 0.11 μM), TAAR1 (EC50 about 1–3 μM), sigma-1 receptor (Ki about 2 μM) and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors (Ki about 1 μM) (refs 15–19). Doses and schedules of the animal and cell studies are not given. Intravenous methamphetamine is said to accumulate mainly in the lung (refs 34, 35).
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed. The review does not mention tobacco, alcohol, cocaine or other drug use as a possible confounder of any cited human association.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Of the cited human figures, only the 1999 autopsy comparison (19% versus 0.5% in sex- and age-matched controls, ref 40) and the 20-versus-21 vasodilation study (ref 31) are described with a comparison group; the Australian autopsy figures are said not to have been seen in control cohorts without saying who those were.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. Pre-existing cardiovascular risk (family history, hypertension, smoking, lipids) is not addressed for any cited human study; the review only remarks, without a citation, that methamphetamine use lowers serum cholesterol and obesity.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported for any cited study.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable at review level. Outcomes discussed: heart rate and blood pressure, arterial constriction and vasodilator response, pulmonary hypertension, coronary atherosclerosis at autopsy, sudden cardiac death in records, QT interval on 12-lead ECG, ventricular fibrosis on endomyocardial biopsy and cardiac MRI, dilated cardiomyopathy and its recovery after stopping use.
outcomes.operationalization: Not defined. The review does not give the cited studies' definitions of sudden cardiac death, of 'minimal to severe' or 'extremely severe' coronary disease, or of methamphetamine-associated cardiomyopathy or pulmonary hypertension.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed by the review. Second-hand figures, all without intervals: coronary atherosclerosis in 19% of methamphetamine-related deaths versus 0.5% of sex- and age-matched controls (ref 40); coronary artery disease in 54% and extremely severe coronary disease in up to 10% in two Australian autopsy series (refs 14, 41; which figure comes from which is not stated); a 27% increased risk of sudden cardiac death in a US National Inpatient Sample analysis of more than 35 million patients including over 180,000 who used methamphetamine (ref 49); 6.5% of non-accidental deaths in people who used methamphetamine attributed to sudden cardiac death in Australian coronial data (ref 50); reduced nitroglycerin-mediated vasodilation in 20 people who used methamphetamine versus 21 age-matched controls (ref 31, magnitude not given). The 27% figure has no stated comparator, adjustment, interval or absolute risk.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed (no eligibility criteria or list of considered studies). No cited human study is reported with a null result; absence of evidence is acknowledged for chronic systemic hypertension and for prospective arrhythmia incidence. The meeting abstract cited as ref 49 is titled as reporting stroke as well as sudden cardiac death; the review reports only the sudden-death result.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The human evidence actually cited is autopsy and coronial series, one inpatient-database meeting abstract, case reports and clinical series, one 20-versus-21 vasodilation study and one ECG study; the mechanistic account rests mainly on rodent, rat-aorta and cell-culture experiments. In the body, the authors say the mechanisms remain largely unknown, that most sudden-death figures are biased by retrospective adjudication from records, that no prospective study of arrhythmia incidence exists, and (in the closing paragraph) that the prevalence of methamphetamine-associated cardiovascular pathology still needs systematic study.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract ranks cardiovascular disease as the leading cause of death in people who use methamphetamine after overdose and accidents and attributes it to methamphetamine's effects on vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension, plaque formation, arrhythmias and cardiomyopathy, without figures. The atherosclerosis section opens by saying methamphetamine use "clearly increases the rate of coronary artery disease", on the basis of unadjusted autopsy comparisons, and calls the apolipoprotein-E-knockout mouse experiments direct evidence linking methamphetamine use to plaque formation. The summary says methamphetamine use clearly induces cardiovascular dysfunction, that its acute effects often result in myocardial infarction (no citation or frequency) and that it significantly enhances susceptibility to pulmonary hypertension (no statistic; one cited genetic study whose sample size is not given). The highlights state mechanisms (vasospasm plus plaque in myocardial infarction; remodelling leading to dilated cardiomyopathy) as established. The causal and frequency language of the abstract, summary and highlights is stronger than the observational, selected, unadjusted or non-human evidence in the body, and stronger than the authors' own caveats.

timeline.event: Karch, Stephens & Ho: autopsy series of methamphetamine-related deaths (San Francisco, by title); cited here (ref 40) for coronary atherosclerosis in 19% versus 0.5% of controls

Kaye, Darke, Duflou & McKetin: Australian methamphetamine-related fatalities with major organ pathology; cited here (ref 41) with ref 14 for coronary disease in 54% and extremely severe disease in up to 10%

Darke, Duflou & Kaye national study of cardiovascular disease in methamphetamine-related death (ref 14), and Darke, Kaye & Duflou 7-year national coronial study (ref 50: 6.5% of non-accidental deaths attributed to sudden cardiac death)

Schürer et al.: clinical and histopathological series of methamphetamine-associated cardiomyopathy; cited here (ref 55) for fibrosis related to duration of use and predicting recovery after stopping, and for no improvement in anyone who continued use
Parekh et al. meeting abstract (JACC Cardiovascular Interventions supplement) on the US National Inpatient Sample: 27% increased risk of sudden cardiac death; cited here as ref 49

Hemphill et al. stroke review cites this review (its ref 12) for vasoconstriction, TAAR1 and cardiotoxicity after acute, chronic and binge use; the last statement is uncited here, so the chain of citation ends without a primary source

replication.where_it_stands: A mechanistic overview written by vascular biologists. For any claim about how often cardiovascular disease occurs in people who use methamphetamine, or how much methamphetamine raises the risk, the primary studies (the autopsy and coronial series of Karch 1999, Kaye 2008 and Darke 2017; Schürer 2017; the inpatient-sample analysis, which exists here only as a meeting abstract) need their own cards. The authors' closing statement that prevalence and mechanisms remain to be established should govern how this review is cited.

funding.funder: NIH National Institute of General Medical Sciences Institutional Development Award (IDeA) P20GM121307 to C.G.K.; NIH R01 HL098435, HL133497 and HL141155 to A.W.O.; HL131844 to M.D.W.; HL122354 and HL145753 to M.S.B. (Acknowledgments › Sources of Funding).
funding.affiliations_note: All nine authors are at LSU Health Sciences Center, Shreveport (pathology and translational pathobiology, physiology, cell biology and anatomy, pharmacology and toxicology, microbiology and immunology, medicine). Ref 44, cited for the general description of atherosclerosis, is from two of the authors' own group (Orr, Woolard). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use methamphetamine and a comparison group matched on age, sex, smoking and other stimulant use, with toxicology-verified exposure and repeated echocardiography, ECG and coronary imaging, reporting incident cardiomyopathy, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmia and coronary events as absolute rates; and, for the causal pathway, within-person follow-up of cardiac structure and function after people stop using.

domains.domain: Item 1: research question and inclusion criteria include population, exposure, comparator and outcome
domains.note: The aim is to summarize the literature on four topics; no question in PICO form.

domains.domain: Item 2 (critical): protocol established before the review
Item 3: choice of study designs explained
Item 7 (critical): list of excluded studies with reasons
Item 8: included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Sample sizes are given for only two human studies (20 versus 21; the inpatient sample); design, setting and exposure measurement are not given for any.

domains.domain: Item 9 (critical): satisfactory technique for assessing risk of bias in individual studies
domains.note: Only a one-sentence remark that most sudden-death studies are biased by retrospective record adjudication.

domains.domain: Item 10: funding sources of included studies reported
Item 13 (critical): risk of bias accounted for when interpreting results
domains.note: Caveats in the body are not carried into the abstract, summary or highlights, which use causal language.
One conflict between two cardiomyocyte studies is noted (reduced versus increased L-type calcium activity); human heterogeneity is not discussed.

domains.domain: Item 16: conflicts of interest and funding of the review reported

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A narrative review that does not claim to be systematic; it fails all five applicable AMSTAR 2 critical items (items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply because there is no meta-analysis). Useful as a map of proposed mechanisms and as a pointer to primary studies; every frequency or risk figure in it must be taken from the primary source, and its causal statements about human disease rest on autopsy series, case reports and non-human experiments.

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular disease is described as the second leading cause of death in people who use methamphetamine, after accidental overdose (ref 14, Darke, Duflou & Kaye 2017); no proportion of deaths is given.
key_findings.note: The abstract ranks it after overdose and accidents; the introduction after accidental overdose only. See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Binding values cited: dopamine transporter Ki 0.46 μM, noradrenaline transporter Ki 0.11 μM (ref 15); TAAR1 EC50 about 1–3 μM, sigma-1 receptor Ki about 2 μM, alpha-2 adrenergic receptor Ki about 1 μM (refs 16–19). Blood concentrations cited: average 2–3 μM in people who use methamphetamine, up to 17 μM in people arrested for erratic behaviour, 87 μM in post-mortem samples from deaths not due to overdose (refs 21–23). The authors conclude that human plasma levels are sufficient to engage all these sites.
key_findings.note: Which concentration comes from which of refs 21–23 is not stated, and the review does not discuss whether post-mortem values are comparable with plasma values in living people. Ref 19 (1977) is by title a characterization of alpha-noradrenergic receptor binding that does not name methamphetamine.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine given to people acutely raises heart rate and blood pressure (ref 24). In mice, acute exposure constricted pial and intracerebral arteries (refs 25, 26) and chronic exposure produced vasoconstriction with persistent cerebral hypoperfusion (ref 27). Proposed mechanisms: endothelial endothelin-1 release (ref 25) or arterial TAAR1 signalling (ref 29), with neuronal catecholamine and adrenergic receptor signalling apparently not involved (ref 30).
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-mediated vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Refs 29 and 30 are, by title, rat-aorta studies of trace amines (beta-phenylethylamine) and amphetamines.

key_findings.finding: In 20 people who used methamphetamine and 21 age-matched controls, nitroglycerin-mediated vasodilation was reduced in the methamphetamine group (ref 31, Nabaei et al. 2016); the authors infer smooth-muscle dysfunction and reduced nitric-oxide sensitivity. No magnitude, test statistic or adjustment is reported.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-mediated vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: A cross-sectional comparison; the inference that methamphetamine caused the dysfunction is the review's.

key_findings.finding: Evidence for chronic systemic hypertension is described as minimal; pulmonary hypertension is linked to prolonged use (refs 32, 33: a three-page 1993 report and a 2006 study asking whether methamphetamine use is associated with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension). Nearly all patients with methamphetamine-associated pulmonary hypertension examined in one study carried one copy of a carboxylesterase 1 variant predicted to lower its activity (ref 34); the number examined is not given.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-mediated vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension, 2nd paragraph (after Figure 2)
key_findings.note: The summary turns this into methamphetamine use significantly enhancing susceptibility to pulmonary hypertension, with no statistic.

key_findings.finding: Autopsy evidence: a 1999 study reported minimal-to-severe coronary atherosclerosis in 19% of decedents who had used methamphetamine versus 0.5% of sex- and age-matched controls (ref 40); two Australian autopsy studies reported coronary artery disease in 54% and extremely severe disease in up to 10%, said not to occur in control cohorts (refs 14, 41). Chronic methamphetamine increased atherosclerosis in apolipoprotein-E-knockout mice (refs 42, 43).
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Unadjusted autopsy proportions; the review does not give denominators, ages, smoking or other drug use. The text places the 1999 decedents in southern California; ref 40's title names San Francisco.

key_findings.finding: Proposed atherogenic mechanisms come from mice and cells: endothelial permeability and pro-inflammatory gene expression (refs 45, 46), raised ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and MCP-1 mRNA in treated mice (refs 42, 43), macrophage ROS, IL-6 and IL-1β (ref 47), mitochondrial ROS (ref 48), and plaque features (more smooth muscle, raised interferon-gamma, lower TGF-beta) read as a vulnerable-plaque phenotype. The authors state little is known about methamphetamine's effect on vascular smooth-muscle phenotype.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Ref 47 is by title a 2002 general review of immunity in atherosclerosis, not a methamphetamine study.

key_findings.finding: Sudden cardiac death: a US National Inpatient Sample analysis of more than 35 million patients, including over 180,000 who used methamphetamine, reported a 27% increased risk (ref 49); Australian coronial data attributed 6.5% of non-accidental deaths in people who used methamphetamine to sudden cardiac death (ref 50). The authors caution that most such studies are biased by retrospective adjudication from records.
key_findings.note: Ref 49 is a meeting abstract (journal supplement page S29, no DOI listed). No interval, comparator definition, adjustment or absolute risk is given for the 27%.

key_findings.finding: No prospective observational study of arrhythmia incidence in people who use methamphetamine exists, according to the authors; evidence consists of isolated case reports of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (ref 51), QT prolongation on 12-lead ECG (ref 52, one study, described as growing evidence), and one animal study in which atrial and ventricular ectopic beats and sinus tachycardia occurred in the 30 minutes after methamphetamine, without sustained ventricular arrhythmias (ref 53).
key_findings.note: Ref 53 is by title a study of electronic control device exposure in a methamphetamine-intoxicated animal model, not a study designed around cardiac rhythm alone.

key_findings.finding: Structural and electrical remodelling: biopsies in methamphetamine-associated cardiomyopathy showed inflammation and fibrosis (sentence uncited); ventricular fibrosis was corroborated by cardiac MRI (ref 54); the extent of fibrosis correlated with duration of use and predicted recovery after stopping (ref 55). In animals, potassium and L-type calcium channel expression fell and largely recovered by week 8 of withdrawal (ref 56); in isolated rat myocytes, methamphetamine inhibited potassium and L-type calcium currents dose-dependently (ref 57), while another study found increased beating rate and calcium sparks (ref 58).
key_findings.note: No numbers are given for the correlation between fibrosis and duration of use.

key_findings.finding: Cardiomyopathy: methamphetamine-associated cardiomyopathy is described as severe systolic dysfunction with left-ventricular dilation (refs 55, 59), most commonly dilated (ref 61); clinical and autopsy reports describe necrosis, fibrosis, hypertrophy and cardiac enlargement (ref 60); in one series the degree of fibrosis predicted recovery after stopping use, and cardiac function did not improve in any patient who continued use (ref 55). Rat studies show myocyte disarray, oedema, abnormal mitochondria and myofilament loss (ref 62).
key_findings.note: No numbers of patients, recovery proportions or follow-up times are given.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that proposed mechanisms of methamphetamine cardiomyopathy (catecholamine excess, ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction, vasospasm, ischaemia) are "primarily based on cursory observations" and that the molecular targets remain unknown; isolated-cardiomyocyte studies are taken as support for direct, catecholamine-independent toxicity (refs 57, 63, 64).
The authors conclude that methamphetamine-associated cardiovascular complications need systematic study to establish the prevalence of pathology and the mechanisms of disease progression.

reporting_issues.issue: The 1999 autopsy study is described as a study of decedents from southern California, but the cited paper (ref 40, Karch, Stephens & Ho 1999) is titled as a study of methamphetamine-related deaths in San Francisco.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the location or the citation is wrong; the 19% versus 0.5% figures must be checked in the primary paper before use.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements carry no citation: a case report of vasospasm-related myocardial infarction unresponsive to vasodilators; methamphetamine use lowering serum cholesterol and obesity; increased T cells and macrophages in plaques of treated mice (only Figure 2B is referenced); biopsy findings of inflammation and fibrosis in methamphetamine cardiomyopathy; cardiotoxicity after acute, chronic and binge administration; and, in the summary, acute effects often resulting in myocardial infarction.
reporting_issues.consequence: None of these statements can be traced to a source from this review; they cannot support claims.

reporting_issues.issue: Citations that do not match their claims by title: the figure of up to 51 million people worldwide using amphetamine-type stimulants is cited to two psychosis papers (refs 8, 9: McKetin et al. 2013; Wearne & Cornish 2018) rather than an epidemiological source; macrophage production of ROS, IL-6 and IL-1β after methamphetamine is cited to a 2002 general review of immunity in atherosclerosis (ref 47); an alpha-2 adrenergic Ki for methamphetamine is cited to a 1977 receptor-binding characterization (ref 19); the TAAR1 vasoconstriction mechanism is cited to a beta-phenylethylamine rat-aorta study (ref 29); the only animal study of the acute effect on cardiac rhythm is a study of electronic control device exposure (ref 53).
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements need their primary sources; the global prevalence figure should come from UNODC or equivalent, not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract places cardiovascular disease after overdose and accidents as a cause of death; the introduction calls it second only to accidental overdose. Neither gives a proportion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The ranking cannot be cited from this review; the coronial data (Darke et al. 2017) should be used directly.

reporting_issues.issue: The 27% increased risk of sudden cardiac death is reported as demonstrated by a database analysis of more than 35 million patients; the source (ref 49) is a meeting abstract in a journal supplement, and the review gives no comparator, adjustment, interval or definition of sudden cardiac death in an inpatient database.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as a risk estimate without the full analysis; a relative figure without a base rate cannot be turned into absolute risk.

reporting_issues.issue: Read from the PMC author manuscript, which may differ from the published version (Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol 2019;39(9):1739–1746); printed pagination is not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors are to sections and paragraphs of the author manuscript.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6709697 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, highlights, both figure legends, sources of funding, disclosures, author affiliations and the full reference list; Figures 1–2 and the graphical abstract are images and were not extracted; no supplementary material)
